content: Fluocinolone acetonide is a topical corticosteroid approved by the FDA for the treatment of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. Common adverse reactions include burning, itching, irritation, dryness, and folliculitis. For adults, fluocinolone acetonide cream is indicated to relieve inflammatory and pruritic symptoms associated with corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. The cream is typically applied as a thin film to the affected area two to four times daily, depending on the severity of the condition. In areas with hair, the hair should be parted to allow direct contact with the lesion. Occlusive dressings may be used for managing psoriasis or recalcitrant conditions, but caution is advised as some plastic films may be flammable. Care should also be taken to avoid accidental suffocation when such films are used on children or left near them. If an infection develops, occlusive dressings should be discontinued, and appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be initiated. There is limited information regarding off-label guideline-supported use of fluocinolone acetonide in adults. However, it has been used off-label for conditions such as vitiligo. For pediatric patients, there is limited information on FDA-labeled or off-label uses of fluocinolone acetonide. Pediatric patients are more susceptible to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome due to their larger skin surface area relative to body weight. Adrenal suppression in children may manifest as growth retardation, delayed weight gain, low plasma cortisol levels, and lack of response to ACTH stimulation. Intracranial hypertension may present as bulging fontanelles, headaches, and bilateral papilledema. Topical corticosteroid use in children should be limited to the smallest amount necessary for effective treatment, as chronic use may interfere with growth and development. Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to any components of the preparation. There is limited information on specific warnings for fluocinolone acetonide in the drug label. Adverse reactions reported with topical corticosteroids include burning, itching, irritation, dryness, and folliculitis. These reactions may occur more frequently with the use of occlusive dressings. During pregnancy, fluocinolone acetonide is classified as Category C by the FDA. Corticosteroids have been shown to be teratogenic in laboratory animals when administered systemically at low doses. Potent corticosteroids have demonstrated teratogenic effects after dermal application in animals. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, so topical corticosteroids should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. They should not be used extensively, in large amounts, or for prolonged periods in pregnant patients. There is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on its use in pregnancy. There is no FDA guidance on the use of fluocinolone acetonide during labor and delivery. It is unknown whether topical administration of corticosteroids results in sufficient systemic absorption to produce detectable quantities in breast milk. Systemically administered corticosteroids are secreted into breast milk in quantities unlikely to harm the infant. However, caution should be exercised when administering topical corticosteroids to nursing women. There is no FDA guidance on the use of fluocinolone acetonide in geriatric patients, specific gender populations, racial populations, patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. Topical corticosteroids can be absorbed through normal intact skin, and absorption is increased in the presence of inflammation, skin disease, or occlusive dressings. Once absorbed, they are metabolized primarily in the liver and excreted by the kidneys, with some excretion into bile. Long-term animal studies have not been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic or fertility effects of topical corticosteroids. Studies on mutagenicity with prednisolone and hydrocortisone have shown negative results. Fluocinolone acetonide cream should be stored at room temperature (15–25°C or 59–77°F) and protected from freezing and excessive heat above 40°C (104°F). There is no established interaction between alcohol and fluocinolone acetonide, but patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication.
